title: His first record with Armstrong, the Billy May tuba obbligato, and MGM film work
summary: He recalls "Once In A While" as his first record and a Nat Cole album with a tuba obbligato, then work at MGM with Lee Young and Lena Horne.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: My first record date: sessions, personnel, discography

blocks.x: Charlie Harris, who lives in Baltimore. The reason I got to play with so many different bass players is because of playing the tuba. I was listening to one thing, "Once In A While," where Billy May had me featured behind Nat Cole; I was playing like an obbligato on the tuba to the bridge of "Once In A While." And that happens to be one of my favorite things. "Once In A While," incidentally, happens to be the first record I ever made, and that was with Louis Armstrong on Decca. That was in 1937, when I played with Louis when Pops Foster got sick. Elmer Fain said, "Hey, kid, do you want to want to work with Louis?" I couldn't believe it.
You really started at the top, right?

Well, I would like to think so. But it's funny, because being so young and working with all these guys gave me a lot of confidence. I said, "God, if I can play with these guys, I can do anything." So fortunately,

it brought me to the notice of a lot of people. Like, I worked at MGM with Hazel Scott. This was a little later, but I did a picture, I Dood It, you know, which I was so young, you wouldn't even recognize me now -- with Lee Young and I. Lee was under contract to Columbia Studios, which very few people knew. This was before it was fashionable to hire Black musicians, you know. But Lee was under contract to Columbia and I did a lot of work at MGM with Lennie Hayden and Lena Horne and whoever happened to be there.
